A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Q-Adapter and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared formulation, algorithm, and experiments can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original DSP and HH-RLHF experiments in Tables 1–2, preference evaluations and hyperparameter analysis in Figures 2–3, and generated responses in Appendix D.

after.justification: V2 reports original DSP and HH-RLHF experiments, training-checkpoint evaluations, hyperparameter analyses, and generated responses in Tables 1–2, Figures 2–4 and 6, and Appendices D–E.

M1.justification: V2 Equation (10) corrects the regularization sign in v1 Equation (9), making the squared-reward term a positive loss penalty. V1 Appendix C already implemented a positive penalty, so this establishes a correction to the documented loss, not a newly introduced component. The residual-Q adapter, preference-learning procedure, and policy-composition rule otherwise remain.

E1.justification: The four DSP domains and helpful-to-harmless HH-RLHF transfer remain. MathQA and HumanEval are removed, while MMLU Pro, BBH, and IFEval introduce harder knowledge questions, additional reasoning tasks, and explicit instruction-following evaluation. MMLU and GSM8K coverage remains; replacing their Tiny evaluations belongs to protocol changes.

E2.justification: Replay is newly evaluated in both DSP and HH-RLHF, adding a comparison family directly relevant to forgetting mitigation. PPO appears in v1's HH-RLHF Table 2 but is omitted from v2's corresponding comparison because of training instability. DSP retains SFT, DPO, and PPO; the PR labels rename the latter two.

E3.justification: The reported base model changes from Llama-3 8B to Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and LoRA rank changes from 16 to 8. Table 3 changes alpha-tilde from 0.1 to 1, alpha0 from 1 to 0.01, and gamma from 0.99 to 1. TinyMMLU/TinyGSM8K evaluations are replaced by standard benchmark tasks. Preference judging changes from GPT-4-turbo against the base model to GPT-4o against SFT, and the alpha0 sweep uses different values and scoring.

E4.justification: V2 adds training-checkpoint MMLU curves testing how forgetting develops (Figure 2) and a beta sweep testing the contribution and sensitivity of reward regularization (Appendix D, Figure 6). It revises the existing alpha0 tradeoff analysis and expands qualitative analysis to DSP style examples while replacing the HH-RLHF response case.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experiments. The revised tables and plots continue to present point estimates.

E6.justification: The main benchmark and preference results are replaced under changed conditions. V1 Figure 2 reports DSP win rates against the base model; v2 Table 2 reports Q-Adapter's SFT-relative rates of 55.59%, 53.84%, 63.77%, and 58.20% across the four domains. V2 also replaces HH-RLHF results and adds checkpoint and beta findings. These are new or replaced measurements, not directly comparable performance gains, because models and evaluation protocols differ.

T1.justification: V2 replaces v1's incorrectly indexed soft-Q recursion with a discounted-return definition and adds a proof of the KL-regularized/maximum-entropy equivalence in Appendix A.1. Corollary 4.1 gains an explicit proof of the reward–residual-Q correspondence. The main residual-Q derivations remain, while v1's soft-optimality proof is replaced by a cited lemma.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a reward-sum formulation of customization, direct learning of a residual-Q adapter without separately learning reward models, and mitigation of forgetting while learning new preferences. The rewritten abstract, title, and contribution list retain these central claims.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes DSP performance often matching or exceeding the base model; v2 interprets its results as reduced forgetting despite remaining benchmark losses. V2 also recognizes Replay as competitive on HH-RLHF, identifies instability at large alpha0, and explains beta regularization as stabilizing training. The limitations concerning RLHF-trained base models and only one demonstrated customization round remain.

D1.justification: V2 Appendices B–C substantially expand baseline implementation, base-model preparation, benchmark task names, prompting and scoring configurations, and the judging prompt, explicitly documenting length-controlled win rates. Hyperparameters and the training-time estimate are revised. However, v1's training-loss code and some microbatch, memory, and DeepSpeed details disappear. The Q-Adapter repository address remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 makes attribution to residual Q-learning more explicit through Section 2.3 and Proposition 2.2; v1 already cited and followed Li et al. It adds personalization, customization, forgetting, retrieval, and benchmark references, including Salemi, Wozniak, Liu, and Luo, while removing several earlier references. The central positioning relative to RLHF, DPO, IPL, and LoRA remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Residual Q-learning becomes a preliminary subsection, customization formalization and Q-Adapter receive separate sections, and related work moves after experiments. The appendices are reorganized and subdivided, the Broader Impacts appendix is removed, and the title and author information change.

P2.justification: The original framework diagram moves from v1 Figure 1 to v2 Figure 5, alongside a new introductory illustration. DSP win rates change from a bar chart to a table, HH-RLHF results from a table to a scatter plot, and alpha0 analysis from a scatter plot to grouped bars. Checkpoint and beta plots are added, with substantial table and document-template changes.

improvement.justification: The added Replay comparison and training-checkpoint analysis substantially strengthen testing of the central forgetting-mitigation claim. The beta ablation and detailed benchmark/judge specifications address important gaps in v1's empirical justification and reproducibility, while formula corrections improve mathematical consistency. Removing coding evaluation, HH-RLHF general-benchmark results, and its PPO comparison narrows some evidence, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported. Nevertheless, the gains in testing and documenting the main contribution are substantial.
